d.x: Scientists debunk the myth that gum stays in the human stomach for seven years.

d.g: A person or thing held in excessive or quasi-religious awe or admiration based on popular legend
d.x: Father Flanagan was legendary, his institution an American myth. (Tucson (Arizona) Citizen, 20 September 1979, 5A/3, cited after OED)

myth.e: From Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “word, humour, companion, speech, account, rumour, fable”). Attested in English since 1830. Doublet of mythos.

d.g: Alternative form of mythologization.
A person who studies mythology

The collection of myths of a people, concerning the origin of the people, history, deities, ancestors and heroes.
A similar body of myths concerning an event, person or institution.
Pervasive elements of a fictional universe that resemble a mythological universe.
d.x: This tongue-in-cheek episode is especially fun for people who don’t take their “X-Files” mythology seriously.

d.g: The set of misconceptions and false attitudes that are held about something and contribute to its perception.

mythology.e: First attested as Middle English in 1412. From Middle French mythologie, from Latin mythologia, from Ancient Greek μυθολογία (muthología, “legend”) μυθολογέω (muthologéō, “to tell tales”), from μυθολόγος (muthológos, “legend”), from μῦθος (mûthos, “story”) + λέγω (légō, “to say”). …

myxovirus.e: From myxo- + virus, from Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “mucus”), because they react with mucin (mucoprotein) on the surface of red blood cells.

d.g: To thoroughly confuse, befuddle, or bewilder.

mystify.e: From French mystifier, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”) + Latin -ficare.
